idiom_name: Monitor (or MonitorMixin) around the guarded state; Thread::Mutex for the bare form
implementation_notes: Ruby ships the pattern as a class: the documentation says to 'use the Monitor class when you want to have a lock object for blocks with mutual exclusion', and Monitor brings `synchronize`, `try_enter` and condition variables (`new_cond`) on the same object - a reentrant guardian whose lock is private to whoever holds a reference. `MonitorMixin` goes one step further and makes the guarded object itself its own monitor, which is the idiomatic Ruby form when the state lives in a class; `Thread::Mutex` is the raw non-reentrant alternative with `synchronize` as its block form, and `Thread::Queue`/`SizedQueue` replace locking entirely by handing the state to one consumer. What is genuinely different from the classic structure is that the language provides the whole guardian, so the work is choosing the right one and keeping the guarded state from escaping.
pitfalls: MRI's GVL makes many operations look atomic, so `@total += delta` without `synchronize` passes tests and still loses updates on JRuby/TruffleRuby or whenever the guarded region awaits I/O - the GVL is not the guardian.

`MonitorMixin` changes the class protocol: `initialize` must call `super`, and including it into a frozen object or one that already uses a `Mutex` breaks `synchronize` (a `Mutex` is not reentrant, a `Monitor` is).
A guarded block that calls out to other code can deadlock against a second monitor; keep callbacks, I/O and foreign service calls outside the `synchronize` block.
